newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria Q2 oil, gas industry output up 9.2 percent. [CORRECTED 01:25 GMT 7/11]
newsitem.headline: Algeria Q2 oil, gas industry output up 9.2 percent. [CORRECTED 01:25 GMT 7/11]

text.p: Algeria's oil and gas industry recorded output growth of 9.2 percent in the second quarter (corrects from first quarter) of 1996, compared to the same period last year, official figures showed on Wednesday.

"The hydrocarbons sector confirms its recovery which is explained mainly by the increase in output of liquid hydrocarbons, refined products and liquefied gas products due to renovation work on refinery and liquefaction facilities," said the National Statistics Office (ONS), quoted by the official news agency APS.

Oil and gas exports provide the North African OPEC member country with some 95 percent of its foreign earnings. In the first three months of 1996, the sector's output grew at 6.1 percent, compared with the same period last year.

The ONS said non-energy industrial production fell 6.2 percent in the second quarter 1996. In the the first three months of this year the sector's output fell by 2.1 percent compared with the first three months of 1995.
The continuing bad performance by non-energy industry was mostly due to financial problems, the ONS said.

Isolated growth outside oil and gas came in the building materials sector which rose by 2.8 percent in the second quarter of 1996. The ONS gave no comparative figure for the second quarter of 1995 but said the building materials industry output fell by 34 percent in the first half of 1995.
Farm produce output also showed growth, of 4.4 percent in the second quarter of 1996 compared to minus 1.1 percent in the second quarter of 1995, said the ONS.

Algeria forecast Gross Domestic Product growth would rise by 5.2 percent this year and by 5.0 percent in both 1997 and 1998. Earlier government figures showed GDP growth at 4.4 percent in the first half of 1996.

Algeria's Central Bank said last month the country's foreign currency reserves rose to more than $3.5 billion, the highest since 1981 when crude oil prices shot up in the wake of the war between Iran and Iraq.

The government, worried by the continuing slump of the industry other than oil and gas, set up last June several working parties to advise on ways to rescue the ailing sector still controlled by the state and which employs about two-fifths of the five million workforce.
The government has pumped at least 500 billion dinars ($9.0 billion) into non-energy industry over the past seven years to try to save jobs and bolster its transition towards a free market.
Officials blame Moslem guerrillas for some of the bad performance by non-energy industry, through a sabotage campaign which cost the economy more than $2.0 billion.
